note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: 2024 was the hottest year on record. How far above pre-industrial temperatures was it?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.55°C — the first single year to pass the 1.5°C mark that the Paris Agreement aimed to avoid.
whyWrong: Ten times too high — that would be catastrophic.
questions.action: Look up the hottest day ever recorded where you live.

questions.prompt: 2024 was the hottest year in how many years of records?
questions.whyCorrect: 175 years — the entire span of reliable global temperature measurement.
whyWrong: Direct instrument records don't reach that far back.
questions.action: Find out when weather records began in your country.

questions.prompt: What's the chance that one of the next five years beats 2024's heat record?
questions.whyCorrect: 80% — records are now expected to fall regularly rather than rarely. The baseline itself has shifted.
whyWrong: Warming is ongoing, so new records are likely.
questions.action: Ask what it means when records stop being unusual.

questions.prompt: Long-term global warming is currently estimated at:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.34–1.41°C as a long-term trend — lower than 2024's single-year 1.55°C, because individual years bounce around the trend line.
whyWrong: Far above current warming, though possible by 2100.
questions.action: Ask why one hot year doesn't equal the long-term trend.

questions.prompt: Global greenhouse gas emissions in 2023 hit a record:
questions.whyCorrect: 57.1 gigatons — up 1.3% on 2022. Despite three decades of climate talks, emissions have never yet peaked.
questions.action: Ask what year global emissions are expected to peak.

questions.prompt: Which sector emits the most greenhouse gases?
questions.whyCorrect: Power generation at 26% — well ahead of transport at 15%, and agriculture and industry at 11% each.
whyWrong: Transport is 15% — significant but not the largest.
questions.action: Find out what fuels your country's electricity.

questions.prompt: Transport accounts for what share of global emissions?
questions.whyCorrect: 15% — less than power's 26%, but the hardest to cut, since only about 4% of transport energy is renewable.
questions.action: Count how you travelled this week and how it was powered.

questions.prompt: To stay under 1.5°C, emissions must fall by how much each year until 2035?
questions.whyCorrect: 7.5% every single year — steeper than the drop during the global pandemic shutdowns, sustained for a decade.
questions.action: Ask what a 7.5% yearly cut would change in your life.

questions.prompt: To stay under 2°C instead of 1.5°C, emissions must fall by how much yearly?
questions.whyCorrect: 4% a year — still enormous, but roughly half the 7.5% needed for 1.5°C. Every half-degree of ambition changes the required pace.
questions.action: Compare 7.5% and 4% over ten years.

questions.prompt: Under current policies, how much warming is the world heading for?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.1°C — roughly double the Paris target. Current policies are not close to current promises.
whyWrong: That's the target, not the projection.
questions.action: Ask what 3.1°C would mean for your region.

questions.prompt: How much did governments spend subsidising fossil fuels in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $1.10 trillion — down sharply from $1.68 trillion in 2022, but still nearly three times 2020 levels.
questions.action: Ask why a government would pay to make fuel cheaper.

questions.prompt: Fossil fuel subsidies between 2022 and 2023:
questions.whyCorrect: Fell 34.5%, from $1.68 trillion to $1.10 trillion — real progress, though still triple 2020 levels.
questions.action: Ask what happened to energy prices in 2022.

questions.prompt: How many countries submitted updated climate plans by the 2025 deadline?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 22 countries as of May 2025. Almost every government missed the deadline for their own agreed climate commitments.
questions.action: Look up whether your country submitted a new climate plan.

questions.prompt: What do disasters cost the world economy each year on average?
questions.whyCorrect: $202 billion in direct losses — and $2.3 trillion a year once knock-on effects like lost trade and health costs are counted.
questions.action: Look up the cost of the last major disaster near you.

questions.prompt: Counting knock-on effects, annual disaster costs reach:
questions.whyCorrect: $2.3 trillion — more than eleven times the direct $202 billion, because disasters break supply chains, health and livelihoods for years.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a business after its town floods.

questions.prompt: How many people are affected by disasters each year, per 100,000?
questions.whyCorrect: 2,028 per 100,000 — about 2% of humanity affected annually, and a 75% increase over the previous decade.
questions.action: Work out how many people that is in a city of a million.

questions.prompt: The number of people affected by disasters has risen by:
questions.whyCorrect: 75% more people affected than in the previous decade — even as deaths fell 36%. More disruption, fewer deaths.
whyWrong: Far more people are affected, not fewer.
questions.action: Ask how deaths can fall while impacts rise.

questions.prompt: Disaster deaths compared with the previous decade have:
questions.whyCorrect: Fallen 36%, to about 41,647 a year — a genuine success driven by early warnings and better evacuation, even as disasters got worse.
questions.action: Look up how a cyclone warning saves lives.

questions.prompt: How many people die in disasters each year?
questions.whyCorrect: About 41,647 a year — a rate of 0.79 per 100,000 people, and 36% lower than the previous decade.
questions.action: Ask what makes a disaster deadly versus merely damaging.

questions.prompt: How many countries now have national disaster risk strategies?
questions.whyCorrect: 131, up from just 57 in 2015 — more than doubled. Preparedness is one of the clearest SDG success stories.
questions.action: Find out if your country has a disaster strategy.

questions.prompt: How many countries have multi-hazard early warning systems?
questions.whyCorrect: 113 countries — the main reason disaster deaths fell 36% even as disasters became more frequent and severe.
questions.action: Check how you would be warned of a flood or storm.

questions.prompt: The world's average school 'green curriculum' score is 40. The benchmark is:
questions.whyCorrect: 50 — so schools worldwide are teaching climate at only 80% of the agreed standard.
whyWrong: That's the current score, not the target.
The benchmark is 50, not a perfect score.
questions.action: Count how many climate lessons you had this year.

questions.prompt: What share of countries have NO green content in grade 3 social science?
questions.whyCorrect: 27% — over a quarter of countries teach nothing about the environment to nine-year-olds in social studies.
whyWrong: Too high — most countries do include some content.
questions.action: Look at what your school teaches about climate, and when.

questions.prompt: What share of countries lack green content in grade 9 science?
questions.whyCorrect: 8% — much better than the 27% gap at grade 3. Climate is taught, but often too late.
questions.action: Ask when children should first learn about climate.

questions.prompt: Agriculture and industry each account for what share of global emissions?
questions.whyCorrect: 11% each — together 22%, close to the power sector's 26%. No single sector can solve climate change alone.
questions.action: Add up the four sector percentages given.

questions.prompt: 'Pre-industrial levels' as a temperature baseline means roughly:
options: Before large-scale fossil fuel burning began, around 1850-1900
questions.whyCorrect: Around 1850–1900, before coal-powered industry reshaped the atmosphere. All warming figures are measured from that baseline.
whyWrong: The baseline is over 150 years back.
The world had already warmed considerably by 2000.
questions.action: Look up what year the industrial revolution took off.

questions.prompt: Emissions rose 1.3% from 2022 to 2023. To hit 1.5°C they need to:
questions.whyCorrect: The gap between +1.3% and −7.5% is nearly nine percentage points a year — the single starkest number in Goal 13.
whyWrong: Rising emissions move away from every target.
questions.action: Add 1.3 and 7.5 to see the size of the gap.

questions.prompt: An 'NDC' in climate talks is:
options: A country's own pledge of how much it will cut emissions
questions.whyCorrect: A Nationally Determined Contribution — each country sets its own target. Only 22 had submitted updates by May 2025.
whyWrong: It is a policy commitment, not equipment.
A carbon tax is one possible tool inside an NDC.
questions.action: Look up your country's emissions pledge.

questions.prompt: Fossil fuel subsidies of $1.10 trillion compare with 2020 levels as:
questions.whyCorrect: Nearly three times 2020 levels, despite falling 34.5% from the 2022 peak. Governments still spend enormously to keep fossil fuels cheap.
whyWrong: Subsidies are far higher than in 2020.
questions.action: Ask what $1.1 trillion could buy in clean energy.

questions.prompt: Disaster deaths fell 36% while people affected rose 75%. The best explanation is:
options: Warning systems save lives, but disasters hit more people and destroy more
questions.whyCorrect: 113 countries with early warning systems means people get out in time — but their homes, crops and livelihoods still get destroyed.
whyWrong: Disaster frequency and severity both increased.
questions.action: Ask what an evacuation saves and what it doesn't.

questions.prompt: The disaster mortality rate is 0.79 per 100,000 people. In a city of one million, that's about:
questions.whyCorrect: About 8 a year on the global average — though the real figure clusters heavily in exposed, poorly protected places.
questions.action: Multiply 0.79 by ten to get the per-million rate.

questions.prompt: Countries with disaster strategies more than doubled from 57 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 131 countries since 2015 — one of the strongest improvements across all 17 goals.
whyWrong: More than the number of countries in the world with such plans.
The rise was larger than this.
questions.action: Ask what a national disaster strategy contains.

questions.prompt: The Paris Agreement's central aim is to hold warming to:
questions.whyCorrect: Well below 2°C with efforts toward 1.5°C — which is why 2024 hitting 1.55°C in a single year was such a significant marker.
whyWrong: 3.1°C is the current-policy projection, not the aim.
questions.action: Look up what year the Paris Agreement was signed.

questions.prompt: The gap between current policies (3.1°C) and the Paris goal (1.5°C) is:
questions.whyCorrect: 3.1°C is more than twice 1.5°C. Every tenth of a degree in that gap means more heatwaves, floods and lost coastline.
whyWrong: Policies fall far short of the goal.
questions.action: Subtract 1.5 from 3.1.

questions.prompt: Only 22 countries filed updated climate plans by deadline. This mainly shows:
options: Political commitment lags far behind stated urgency
questions.whyCorrect: The countries that agreed the deadline mostly missed it — the gap between what governments say and what they file is Goal 13's core problem.
whyWrong: Emissions hit a record high in 2023.
It was an agreed obligation under the Paris Agreement.
questions.action: Look up how many countries signed the Paris Agreement.

questions.prompt: The power sector is 26% of emissions. That makes it:
options: The largest single source and the most reduceable, since renewables already work
questions.whyCorrect: Electricity is the easiest sector to decarbonise — renewables already supply 30% of it, versus 4% of transport energy.
whyWrong: It is the single biggest sector.
It is the sector changing fastest.
questions.action: Find out your electricity provider's renewable share.

questions.prompt: A green curriculum score of 40 against a benchmark of 50 means schools are:
questions.whyCorrect: 40 out of 50 is 80% — climate education exists nearly everywhere but is thinner and later than agreed.
whyWrong: The score is below the benchmark.
Most countries teach some green content.
questions.action: Divide 40 by 50.

questions.prompt: $2.3 trillion in annual disaster costs compares with the world economy as roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly 2% of everything the world produces, lost to disasters every year — before counting the human cost.
whyWrong: Far too low for a $2.3 trillion figure.
questions.action: Look up the size of the world economy.

questions.prompt: 27% of countries teach no green content at grade 3, but only 8% at grade 9. This means:
options: Climate is taught, but mostly to older students
questions.whyCorrect: Coverage improves with age — but habits and attitudes form early, so the grade 3 gap matters more than the number suggests.
whyWrong: Most countries do teach it eventually.
Coverage is thinner for younger students.
questions.action: Ask when you first learned what a greenhouse gas is.

questions.prompt: 2024 exceeded 1.5°C in a single year. Does that mean the Paris target is already breached?
options: Not formally — the target refers to a long-term average, currently 1.34-1.41°C
questions.whyCorrect: Paris measures a multi-decade average, not one year. But a single year at 1.55°C is a serious warning that the average is closing in.
whyWrong: One year above does not breach a long-term average.
The 1.5°C aim is in the Paris Agreement text.
questions.action: Ask why scientists use long-term averages.

questions.prompt: Which change in Goal 13 has been most successful?
options: Early warning systems and disaster planning
questions.whyCorrect: Countries with disaster strategies more than doubled to 131, and 113 have early warning systems — cutting deaths 36% despite worse disasters.
whyWrong: Emissions hit a record high in 2023.
Subsidies remain near three times 2020 levels.
questions.action: Find out who issues weather warnings in your country.

questions.prompt: Emissions of 57.1 gigatons CO2-equivalent means:
options: All greenhouse gases converted into their carbon dioxide equivalent
questions.whyCorrect: Methane and nitrous oxide trap far more heat per molecule than CO2, so they are converted to a common CO2-equivalent scale for comparison.
whyWrong: CO2 alone is smaller — about 37.6 gigatons.
Methane is one of several gases included.
questions.action: Look up how much more heat methane traps than CO2.

questions.prompt: The 75% rise in people affected by disasters is driven mainly by:
options: More frequent extreme weather plus more people living in exposed places
questions.whyCorrect: Warming makes extremes more likely, and urban growth pushed more people onto floodplains and coasts — the two multiply.
whyWrong: The trend is consistent across a decade.
Reporting improved, but the physical increase is real.
questions.action: Ask why cities keep building in risky places.

questions.prompt: Ending fossil fuel subsidies would primarily:
options: Make fossil fuels reflect their true cost, freeing money for clean energy
questions.whyCorrect: $1.10 trillion a year currently makes the dirtiest option artificially cheap — removing it is the fastest lever governments hold.
whyWrong: A trillion dollars a year has substantial effect.
It makes renewables relatively more competitive.
questions.action: Ask why removing subsidies is politically difficult.

questions.prompt: The needed 7.5% annual emissions cut compares with the pandemic year drop of about 5-6% as:
options: Larger — and needed every year, not once
questions.whyCorrect: The world's biggest ever single-year emissions fall came from shutting down travel and industry — and it was still smaller than what's needed annually for a decade.
whyWrong: Sustaining it for a decade is far harder than one year.
questions.action: Ask what could cut emissions 7.5% without a shutdown.

questions.prompt: Which is true about disaster impacts and wealth?
options: Poorer countries lose a far larger share of their economy to each disaster
Rich and poor countries suffer identically
questions.whyCorrect: The same storm can cost a rich country a fraction of a percent of GDP and a small island state a large share of its entire economy.
whyWrong: Poorer and small island states are hit hardest proportionally.
questions.action: Look up a hurricane's cost as a share of a small country's GDP.

questions.prompt: 80% probability of a new record in five years mainly tells us:
options: Warming is ongoing, so record heat is now the expected pattern
questions.whyCorrect: When a record has an 80% chance of falling within five years, the climate itself has shifted — records are following the trend, not defying it.
whyWrong: Year-to-year variation sits on top of a clear trend.
2024 was the hottest year in 175 years.
questions.action: Ask what 'the new normal' actually means.

questions.prompt: $202 billion in direct disaster losses versus $2.3 trillion with cascading effects shows:
options: Direct losses are the whole story
The visible damage is a small fraction of the real cost
questions.whyCorrect: Broken bridges are counted; the years of lost income, health and schooling that follow are ten times larger and usually invisible.
whyWrong: They measure different things, and both are valid.
Cascading effects are eleven times larger.
questions.action: List what stops working for a year after a major flood.

questions.prompt: Power (26%), transport (15%), agriculture (11%) and industry (11%) total:
options: 63% of emissions, with the rest spread across other sources
questions.whyCorrect: 63% — buildings, waste and land-use change make up the remainder. No single fix covers even a third of the problem.
whyWrong: These four sectors don't account for everything.
questions.action: Add the four percentages yourself.

questions.prompt: The starkest Goal 13 fact is:
options: Emissions hit a record 57.1 gigatons in the hottest year ever recorded
questions.whyCorrect: 2024 was the hottest year in 175 years, and 2023 emissions were the highest ever measured. The cause is still accelerating alongside the effect.
whyWrong: That is genuine good news — 57 countries to 131.
A real improvement, though subsidies remain near triple 2020.
questions.action: Find one climate action your school could take this term.
